AKHFASH:v2p580#2/r1.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v2p580#2/r1.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v2p580#2/r1.claim: The waw in وما خلق الذكر والأنثى coordinates the day oath with the earlier oath.

TAB-FULL:v24p455#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p455#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p455#2/r1.claim: The night veils the day with darkness and removes its light; the day then clears, shines, and makes visible what night concealed.

TAB-FULL:v24p455#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p455#2/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p455#2/r2.claim: Qatadah calls night and day two great signs that God rotates over creation.

NAHHAS:v5p241/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p241/r3.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p241/r3.claim: The noun is genitive through coordination; the wāw is not an oath.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p286/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p286/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p286/r1.claim: Mujahid says the night grows dark.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p286/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p286/r2.speaker: ابن جبير
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p286/r2.claim: Ibn Jubayr says the night covers and veils.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p286/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p286/r3.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p286/r3.claim: Qatada says night covers and fills all creatures; Mawardi identifies this as an oath.

QUSHAYRI:v3p426/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p426/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p426/r2.claim: The day becomes bright, clear, and manifest; for gnostics, inward lights disclose everything so they need no lamp.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p75#4/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p75#4/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p75#4/r1.claim: Tajalla means the daylight became clear and appeared from among the darkness.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p75#4/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p75#4/r2.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p75#4/r2.claim: The day and night are two great signs that God repeatedly presents to creatures.

WAHIDI-QT:92:2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:92:2/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:92:2/r1.claim: The day appears and becomes visible.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:92:2-7/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:92:2-7/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:92:2-7/r1.claim: The daylight appears and becomes manifest.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p442#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p442#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p442#2/r2.claim: Day appears and becomes distinct from darkness.

KASHSHAF:92:2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:92:2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:92:2/r1.claim: The day becomes manifest when night darkness vanishes.

KASHSHAF:92:2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:92:2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:92:2/r2.claim: Alternatively, daylight becomes clear and uncovered as the sun rises.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p766/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p766/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p766/r2.claim: تجلى means appearing as night's darkness passes, or becoming visible as the sun rises.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p490#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p490#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p490#2/r2.claim: A poetic line illustrates tajalla as emerging into view.

TABRISI:92:2-3/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:92:2-3/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:92:2-3/r11.claim: Day emerges from darkness, enabling livelihood, while night permits rest; their recurrence in both surahs highlights them as signs of divine wisdom.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p145#3/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p145#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p145#3/r1.claim: Daylight becomes clear and emerges from darkness.

RAZI:92:2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:92:2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI:92:2/r1.claim: The day appears as the darkness of night departs.

RAZI:92:2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:92:2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI:92:2/r2.claim: Alternatively, the day appears and is unveiled with sunrise.

RAZI-FULL:v31p179#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p179#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p179#2/r1.claim: Night shelters animals, stills creatures and brings restorative sleep; day removes darkness and sets people, birds and other creatures moving for livelihood. Their alternation serves both work and rest, as 25:62 and 14:33 say.

RAZI-FULL:v31p179#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p179#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p179#2/r3.claim: Day appears when night darkness departs, or when the sun rises and becomes visible.

QURTUBI-FULL:92:2-3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:92:2-3/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:92:2-3/r4.claim: Tajallā means becoming clear and visible, with its light breaking through the night's darkness.

BAYDAWI-FULL:92:1-7/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:92:1-7/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:92:1-7/r2.claim: Day becomes manifest as night’s darkness departs or as the sun rises.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p343#3/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p343#3/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p343#3/r1.claim: Daylight appears as the darkness of night departs.

QASHANI:92:2-6/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:92:2-6/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:92:2-6/r1.claim: The heart is God’s throne, born from night’s ego-darkness and day’s spirit-light; its spirit-facing aspect, the fuʾād, receives realities, while its self-facing breast preserves secrets and forms meanings.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the case of إذا is problematic: coordination either makes the wāws govern both accusative and genitive, or oath wāws create a disputed construction.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r3.claim: The author rejects treating coordinating wāws as governors; the governing case comes from the element governing the first conjunct.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r4.claim: This is coordination of two genitive and accusative pairs, not coordination under two separate governors; he gives مررت بزيد أمس وعمرو اليوم as the parallel.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r5.speaker: سيبويه
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r5.claim: Sibawayh's poetic example coordinates a genitive and nominative with the same case pattern, supporting the author's construction.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r6.speaker: الخليل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r6.claim: Al-Khalīl says the last two wāws join nouns like ordinary coordination, while the first is like the prepositional bāʾ and tāʾ of oath.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p487/r7.claim: The author says al-Khalīl's statement indicates prohibition, contrary to al-Zamakhsharī's claim that the construction is merely disliked.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r1.claim: The surah is Meccan according to the author, Madinan according to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa, with another report that some of it is Madinan.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r2.claim: The surah explains which traits bring the success and failure just mentioned in the previous surah, then warns of the Fire and distinguishes those entering it from those spared.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r4.claim: Tajallā means became clear and appeared, either when night's darkness departed or through the sun's light.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r5.claim: The oaths evoke the night when living creatures take shelter and the day when they spread out.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r6.claim: A poetic line uses jallā in the sense of clearing or revealing something from the face.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r7.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r7.claim: The majority read tajallā as a past-tense verb whose subject is the day.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r8.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r8.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr reads with two tāʾs, referring to the sun.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p491/r9.claim: Another reading has passive tajallā, referring to the sun being made manifest.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p416#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p416#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p416#2/r3.claim: The night oath refers to darkness covering creation and the day oath to its light and brightness; the paired created male and female recalls other creation pairs.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p445#2/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p445#2/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p445#2/r1.claim: After the preceding surah’s account of purified and corrupted souls and Thamud’s fate, people diverge between good and evil while God governs souls through piety and wickedness.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p445#2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p445#2/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p445#2/r3.claim: Day signifies disclosure: sunlight exposes what was hidden and removes all obscurity, suiting public action.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p445#2/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p445#2/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p445#2/r4.claim: Those seeking secrecy choose night and those seeking publicity choose day, whether righteous or wicked.

DURR:92:1/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:92:1/r11.speaker: أبو إسحاق
DURR:92:1/r11.claim: Abu Ishaq reports Abdullah's connected reading: 'By the night when it covers, by the day when it appears, and by the male and female.'

ALUSI-FULL:v30p147#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p147#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p147#2/r1.claim: The day is revealed by the removal of night, or becomes manifest at sunrise; the latter reading pairs well with night covering the sun, while the first suits night covering day or whatever it hides.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p147#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p147#2/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
ALUSI-FULL:v30p147#2/r2.claim: Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr reads with two initial tāʾs and takes the sun as subject.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p147#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p147#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p147#2/r3.claim: Another reading has the tāʾ with ḍamma and the jīm still, likewise taking the pronoun to refer to the sun; the contrast in tense was discussed earlier.

ELMALILI:92:2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:92:2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:92:2/r1.claim: The previous surah swore by the day when it unveils the sun; here the oath is by the day in its own manifestation.

ELMALILI:92:2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:92:2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:92:2/r2.claim: The manifested day alludes to the manifestation of the sun of truth in unity and to the emergence of Islam.

ELMALILI:92:2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:92:2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:92:2/r3.claim: Although the pronouns grammatically refer to night and day, in reality both the covering and the manifestation belong to God.

QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r1.claim: Day appears and brings everything into view, in contrast with night covering and hiding the world; together they form paired oppositions in cosmic cycle, image, qualities, and effects.

QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r2.claim: The cosmic pair is paralleled by the creation of two contrasting sexes, completing the surah’s pattern of paired contrasts.

QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r3.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r3.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r3.claim: Alternation of night and day carries intuitive and reflective meanings: it moves the soul, evokes an unknown universe and its changes, and points to a power managing the cycle.

QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r4.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r4.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:92:2/r4.claim: The precision and persistence of the cycle show a director who also directs human life and does not leave people aimless; the heart recognizes this despite denial.

IBNASHUR:92:2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:92:2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:92:2/r1.claim: Tajalli means clarity, so the verse describes the clarity of daylight, as do the oaths by the sun's brightness and by morning light.

IBNASHUR:92:2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:92:2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:92:2/r2.claim: The wording alludes to night darkness having prevailed before daylight followed it; darkness was the original state of the earth and solar system before God created and lit the sun, which explains dating days from nights.

IBNASHUR:92:2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:92:2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:92:2/r3.claim: The qualification of night and day by their temporal conditions follows the same explanation as the parallel wording in Surat al-Shams.

IBNASHUR:92:4/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:92:4/r1.speaker: علقمة
IBNASHUR:92:4/r1.claim: Alqama reports that he recited the night and day oaths followed by al-dhakar wa-l-untha; Abu al-Darda testified that he heard the Prophet recite this wording.

IBNASHUR:92:4/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:92:4/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:92:4/r2.claim: Al-Kashshaf calls it the Prophet's reading; Ibn Ashur explains that it reflects the early license to recite variant forms, later abrogated by the Prophet's final-life reading adopted by the canonical readers and written in Abu Bakr's codex.

IBNASHUR:92:4/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:92:4/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:92:4/r3.claim: Ibn Ashur refers readers to his sixth introduction for the meaning of the phrase the Prophet's reading.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p379/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p379/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p379/r3.claim: Daylight is described as clear and illuminating, an obvious brilliance perceptible even to sighted observers; تجلي means becoming clear, like the brightness in al-Shams and al-Ḍuḥā.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p379/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p379/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p379/r4.claim: The passage alludes to night darkness as the original state of the solar system and daylight as following the sun's creation; time reckoning accordingly began with nights before days.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p379/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p379/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p379/r5.claim: The time restrictions on night and day follow the explanation of their corresponding oaths in the preceding surah.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p380/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p380/r5.speaker: علقمة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p380/r5.claim: In a report in both Ṣaḥīḥs, Abū al-Dardāʾ asks how Ibn Masʿūd recited the oath; ʿAlqama gives the wording with الذكر والأنثى, and Abū al-Dardāʾ says he heard the Prophet recite it so.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p380/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p380/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p380/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls this the Prophet's reading; Ibn ʿĀshūr explains it as an early permitted variant that was later replaced by the final reading agreed upon by the reciters and written in Abū Bakr's muṣḥaf.

TABATABAI:92:2-7/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:92:2-7/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:92:2-7/r3.claim: The day is said to have become manifest in the past tense while the night “covers” in the present, following the explanation given for the opening of the preceding surah.

BINTSHATI:v2p121/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p121/r6.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p121/r6.claim: The oath's night, daylight, and creation frame divergent earthly endeavors, then contrasting afterlife fates: the denier's fire and the pious giver's satisfaction.

BINTSHATI:v2p99/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p99/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p99/r2.claim: The Quran uses the root for exile from the land in al-Hashr 59:3, divine manifestation to the mountain in al-Araf 7:143, and the Hour being made manifest in 7:187.

BINTSHATI:v2p99/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p99/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p99/r3.claim: The remaining uses concern the illumination of day in al-Shams and al-Layl.

CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-2:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-2:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-2:anmerkung/r1.claim: The night/day oath parallels other early Meccan oaths and is especially close in wording to 91:3–4; the brightening day corresponds to ḍuḥā in 91:1 and 93:1.

CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-2:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-2:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-2:anmerkung/r2.claim: The moment when day gleams corresponds to the ḍuḥā named in 91:1 and 93:1.

CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-3:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-3:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-3:anmerkung/r1.claim: Qur'anic oaths probably draw on a characteristic expression of pre-Islamic soothsayers, a connection not yet sufficiently studied.

CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-3:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-3:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-3:anmerkung/r2.claim: For the structure and function of this oath type, the commentary points to 93:1–2 and its parallels.

CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-4:kommentar/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-4:kommentar/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-4:kommentar/r1.claim: Night/day and male/female form two cosmic oppositions; the second oath enigmatically points to God, who speaks explicitly in the first-person plural in verses 7–10.

CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-4:kommentar/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-4:kommentar/r2.speaker: Neuwirth
CORPUSCORANICUM:92:1-4:kommentar/r2.claim: Neuwirth reads the two elemental pairs as the structural matrix for differing human aims and their corresponding recompense.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p343/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p343/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p343/r1.claim: Sūrah al-Layl pairs with al-Shams; their central themes and inner and outer features correspond so closely that even a general reader can sense the harmony.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p343/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p343/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p343/r2.claim: Al-Layl develops the preceding sūrah’s claim that the soul succeeds through purification by identifying what corrupts it and how it can be protected and purified.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p343/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p343/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p343/r3.claim: Verses 1–4 use evidence from the outer and inner worlds to establish that Judgment must come: the Hereafter is this world’s counterpart and makes it meaningful.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p345/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p345/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p345/r1.claim: Oaths by natural phenomena in the Qur’an are intended to establish a premise.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p346/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p346/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p346/r1.claim: Night and day, like male and female, are complementary pairs whose members fill one another’s void and together serve their created purpose; without a counterpart, their capacities and uses make no sense.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p346/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p346/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p346/r2.claim: The harmony of opposites argues for monotheism and, here, for the Hereafter; 51:49 calls pairs a reminder that this world has a counterpart completing its purpose.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:92:1/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:92:1/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:92:1/r1.claim: These oaths show the worth of the created things and the greatness of their Creator, while directing attention to the coming subject.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p361/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p361/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p361/r1.claim: Using a past verb for a present event makes it vivid and immediate; the author illustrates this with the Prophet's turning toward heaven and the reproach for killing prophets.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p361/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p361/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p361/r2.claim: Arabic grammarians describe this vivid tense shift as transporting the listener to the event or bringing the event to the listener; past verbs have more temporal uses than the single schoolbook past.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p361/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p361/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p361/r3.claim: Contrast makes meanings clearer and more visible; in the opening oath, night covers while day becomes manifest, and the object of يغشى is omitted to keep every possible object in view.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p362/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p362/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p362/r1.claim: Night's covering unfolds gradually, so يغشى is present tense; daylight appears at once at sunrise, so تجلى is past tense, as in the parallel verbs in al-Shams.

STUDYQURAN:92:2/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:92:2/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:92:2/r1.claim: This verse parallels 91:3 and belongs to a recurring sequence of oaths on the alternation of night and day.
